newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OBSTACLES TO S.AFRICAN SHIPS' REGISTER TACKLED.
newsitem.headline: OBSTACLES TO S.AFRICAN SHIPS' REGISTER TACKLED.

text.p: Obstacles in the way of South Africa becoming a sizeable seafaring nation are gradually being dismantled.

With only six of the 69 South African-owned vessels, and no foreign owned ships, on the South African ships' register, many believe that South Africa is missing out on an important opportunity to create jobs for local seafarers.
One of the main obstacles in the way of a sizeable ships' register has long been foreign exchange controls, but with more of these being lifted in July, an important hurdle will have been overcome.
The unattractive ranking of mortgages for ships has been another problem, which is being tackled by the authorities.
Now, the Department of Transport is finalising an investigation into the incentives needed to attract local and foreign shipowners to the South African registry.

University of Stellenbosch academic Henriette van Niekerk, who is examining possible tax incentives for the industry, told Reuters that as many as 50 new jobs could be created for every one ship added to the South African register.
If South African owners could be attracted back to the local register as well as new foreign owners, the jobs created could be considerable provided adequately trained seafarers were available.
Van Niekerk has asked for submissions from interested parties by May 30 and hopes to finalise her proposals by September before submitting them to the Department of Finance for consideration.
Options being considered include a tonnage tax, similar to that in the Netherlands and Norway, which is independent from profits or losses and is based on the size of vessels.
Analysts said that a key factor to the success of any attempt to increase the number of ships registered in South Africa would be the attitude of the unions.

"If the standard rates which the International Transport Federataon imposes on ships under flags of convenience are used as a basis, it is unlikely that there will be much prospect of employment for South African seafarers," said one analyst.

Able seamen are paid about $1,200 a month and, because of the weak rand, this would put their wages way out of kilter with comparable grades in South Africa and would make employing South African seamen totally uncompetitive.
